newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea seizes Hanbo documents, Kim shelves visit.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea seizes Hanbo documents, Kim shelves visit.

text.p: South Korean police raided the home and offices of the founder of the Hanbo Group on Tuesday, and the Justice Ministry slapped a travel ban on top bankers who extended huge loans to the company's failed steel unit.
President Kim Young-sam cancelled a trip to Europe scheduled for March to focus on domestic woes as Hanbo's loan scandal emerged as a major political problem in an election year.
"President Kim planned to visit Hungary, Poland, Turkey and Italy in early March but this plan has been indefinitely postponed," a presidential spokesman said.
Hanbo's flagship, Hanbo Steel Co, defaulted on debt payments last week, triggering a scandal which the opposition calls the biggest financial irregularity in the country's history.
Kim ordered on Monday a probe into $5.8 billion of loans funnelled to Hanbo's shaky steelmaking unit after the opposition said the scandal must have involved government favour.
Police seized documents belonging to Chung Tae-soo, who built South Korea's 14th largest industrial conglomerate now wallowing in a sea of debt.
Hanbo Steel, the nation's second largest steelmaker which is building a huge new facility in the southern town of Tangjin, filed for court receivership to protect it from creditors.
The group's trading arm, Hanbo Corp, also sought court protection and two other units are scheduled to follow.
A prosecution official said police stormed into the personal office and home of Chung and offices of Hanbo Steel and 15 other affiliates to hunt for loan-related documents.
"Search warrants were issued to seize evidence for any financial irregularities," prosecutor Lee Chung-soo said.
The steelmaker borrowed five trillion won ($5.8 billion) from 61 banks and financial institutions, about 20 times its net worth.
"The government today imposed an overseas travel ban on a further 17 people, including the heads of the four banks, over the Hanbo investigation," a Justice Ministry official said.
The banks are Korea First Bank, Cho Hung Bank, Korea Exchange Bank and unlisted Korea Development Bank, which have the biggest exposure to Hanbo Steel.
This brings to 29 the total number of people banned from leaving the country over Hanbo's loan scandal, he added. Others include Chung himself and other Hanbo executives.
It is not the first time Chung has been investigated.
He paid 15 billion won into a slush fund raised by former president Roh Tae-woo, now serving a 17-year jail term for corruption and human rights abuses.
But a Seoul court trying Chung and Roh, along with other tycoons, acquitted Chung on the grounds the money was forcibly extracted.
The ruling New Korea Party said its parliamentary leader met his opposition counterparts to discuss reopening the National Assembly for talks on Hanbo.
The Hanbo scandal has embarrassed Kim's government which is already on the defensive after a botched effort last month to reform labour laws.

The scandal again hammered the stock market on Tuesday, with banking and securities shares losing heavily. The main index lost 1.85 points to end at 662.85, despite measures by the government to boost sentiment.
An outlawed union group said it was abandoning once-a-week strikes on Wednesdays, partly due to economic turmoil caused by the Hanbo collapse.
The Korean Confederation of Trade Unions led almost four weeks of industrial stoppages against new legislation after it was rammed through parliament on December 26.
But it still planned to go ahead with full stoppages starting on February 18 unless the government scrapped the controversial new labour law, a union official said.
President Kim was forced into a humiliating retreat and sent the bill back to parliament for revision. But he has ruled out voiding the bill.
